name: Do Ho Suh
bio: Do Ho Suh (born 1962) studied oriental painting in Seoul before moving to the United States, where he studied at the Rhode Island School of Design and Yale. His best-known works are full-scale replicas of the places he has lived, sewn from translucent polyester fabric: his childhood home in Seoul, his apartment and corridor at 348 West 22nd Street in New York, stairs, doorways and light switches, all rendered in luminous colour and hung so that visitors can walk through them. The fabric makes architecture portable and weightless, like a memory carried from place to place. He also makes works about the individual and the collective, such as fields of tiny figures holding up a floor or a wall, and 'rubbing' works that trace the surfaces of a building in pencil. Fallen Star (2012) at UC San Diego sets a small house tilted on the corner of a campus building.
studyNotes: Memory as a measured copy. He measures his homes precisely, then remakes them in a material that cannot keep them solid.
Translucency changes architecture. Walls you can see through make every room a view of the next one; colour codes each space.
The detail carries the weight. Light switches, door handles and radiators are sewn at full scale, and they are what make the spaces feel lived in.
One and many. The figure works ask how individuals add up to a crowd or a structure; look at how the scale shifts as you move closer.
